KEY MESSAGE 1...Strong easterly winds, heavy rain, 
coastal/tidal flooding and dangerous marine conditions into 
early on Friday as a strong storm system moves through.

As of early Thursday afternoon, an approximate 998 mb sfc 
cyclone was located near northeast NC, with a parent powerful 
closed upper level cyclone centered in vicinity of the TN 
Valley. To our north is a 1041 mb retreating sfc high pressure,
but is creating a tight easterly pressure gradient between the 
high pressure and the aforementioned low pressure near northeast
NC. 

Still on track for deteriorating conditions starting mid to late 
this afternoon, and particularly tonight into the Friday pre-dawn 
hours, as the surface cyclone treks through the coastal mid-Atlantic 
and Southern New England. Strong to potentially damaging easterly 
wind gusts, windswept rain becoming heavy at times, tidal flooding 
and areas of beach erosion, to go along with dangerous strong-gale 
to storm-force wind gusts and seas upwards of 20 ft, remain expected 
in this period. Headlines were generally unchanged, but we did 
opt to upgrade Cape Cod and the Islands to a High Wind Warning 
earlier this morning, as forecast wind guidance has increased 
the 925 mb low- level jet speeds to 85 kt in some more bullish 
guidance, supporting gusts which could clock into the 55-60 mph 
range overnight tonight. 

Rain: Leading edge of the rain shield looks to have made it up to 
Bridgeport CT as of early this afternoon, and will continue to 
spread gradually northward through late this afternoon south of the 
CT-RI-southeast MA Route 6 to I-95 corridor and toward early this 
evening near the MA/VT/NH border. Rainfall turns steady and 
increasingly heavy particularly late tonight and overnight, 
associated with a 1.4"-1.7" southeasterly PWAT plume advecting in. 
This will serve to enhance rain rates especially for the MA/RI 
coastal plain and with a secondary maxima upslope of the Berkshires. 
The strong ridgetop winds leading to a downsloping/rain shadowing 
signature is well depicted in model QPF forecasts, and lesser 
rain totals downwind of the Worcester Hills. The Wood, Pawcatuck
and Taunton Rivers may approach flood stage, and these rivers 
will need to be monitored for possible river flood warnings. 
Pockets of nuisance areas of poor drainage street flooding in 
urban areas could also develop, but not rising to the level of 
rapid- onset flooding. The bulk of the rain falls through the 
early overnight to the pre- dawn hours from south to north, and 
then a dryslot races NE to turn rainfall from steady and locally
heavy rain to a more intermittent, lighter rain. Though we'll 
get some additional lighter rain through Friday, the bulk of the
rain falls tonight to early Friday morning, with 1.5-2.5" rain 
totals shown for central MA/east-central CT eastward to eastern 
MA and RI, with isolated pockets of 3" not out of the question. 
A secondary maxima of 1.5-2 inches along the east slopes of the 
Berkshires. Downsloping in the CT Valley supports rain totals 
ranging from 0.75"-1.25".

Strong Winds: Guidance today continued to increase the 925 mb 
jet hugging the eastern/southeast coast to nearly 85 kt between 
03-09z Friday. This warrants maintaining the previous Wind 
Advisories for the coasts with gusts up to 50 mph, but the 
potential for stronger gusts in the 55 to 60 mph range for Block
Island, Cape Cod and the Islands. Note that as rain tapers off 
and the dryslot moves through, there could be a second 
resurgence in gusts for a brief period of time, and it is 
possible that the easterly/southeast gusts could be at their 
strongest around or shortly after rain intensity begins to taper
off. The Wind Advisories for interior Southern New England 
really key on the higher elevations and ridgetops, with easterly
jet of 50-65 kt in a stable thermo profile supporting enhanced 
channeled or downslope winds capable of minor wind damage late 
tonight into overnight. There isn't too much foliage left on the
trees but we still expect some pockets of tree and powerline 
damage in the Wind Advisory areas, and possibly a greater/more 
concentrated number of tree and powerline damage reports in the 
High Wind Warning areas. Outside the wind headline areas, expect
easterly wind gusts in the 35 to 40 mph range. Once winds shift
to SW toward daybreak Friday morning, expect gusts to decrease 
rather markedly.

Tidal/Coastal Flooding: No significant changes noted on the 
coastal flooding aspect of the storm, and though minor flooding 
is anticipated, significant or substantial coastal flooding 
isn't expected. We continue to see the peak storm surge of 1.5-2
ft centered tonight into the overnight hours, though wave 
action/wave run-up could also contribute a bit, beyond just the 
storm tide elements. The peak storm surge is expected to occur 
during the lower of the two high tide cycles on both the east 
and southern coasts. While astro tides are higher during the
